patient.name: Kwame Asante
patient.complaint: Sudden severe upper abdominal pain that has spread across his whole abdomen
background: Osteoarthritis of both knees; taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for months
Months of epigastric discomfort eased by antacids
Smokes 20 a day; drinks 20 units a week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with sudden epigastric pain becoming generalised, a rigid abdomen and NSAID use, or a 'most likely cause' twist such as typhoid or metoclopramide.

points: Kwame, 64, on **ibuprofen** for months for his knees.
At 6 am: sudden, severe **epigastric** pain, 'like being stabbed'.
Within two hours the pain spread over his whole abdomen.
He is lying completely still; any movement is agony.

visual.title: Where Kwame's pain started
visual.caption: Acute epigastric pain that then spreads across the abdomen as gastric contents leak into the peritoneum.

steps.lead: Kwame's stomach or duodenal wall has torn right through: a **full-thickness** breach, and peptic ulcer is the commonest cause.

points: Abdomen **rigid like a board**, with guarding everywhere.
Pain worse when he breathes or the trolley moves.

steps.lead: Kwame has generalised **peritonitis**: board-like rigidity, guarding, tachycardia and fever. His normal BP is no comfort, as **hypotension is late**.

steps.q: Which detail in Kwame's history most points to a perforated peptic ulcer?
steps.r: Chronic **NSAID** use is the classic cause, along with H. pylori.

steps.lead: Kwame fits the **perforated peptic ulcer** picture exactly. The notes add **typhoid** as a cause of ileal perforation in a returning traveller.
Kwame is not obstructed, but remember: **metoclopramide** in mechanical bowel obstruction raises pressure and can cause perforation, so avoid it.

steps.text: A mildly raised amylase does not make this pancreatitis: perforation can raise it too. **Rigidity plus sudden onset** means image for free air.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (erect chest X-ray for free air under the diaphragm) or the most specific test (CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast).

steps.lead: Kwame gets an **ABCDE** assessment, urgent surgical review, bloods and an **erect chest X-ray**, the first test for a perforated ulcer.

steps.q: What is the first imaging test for Kwame?
steps.r: **Erect CXR** shows free air under the diaphragm. Endoscopy is dangerous with a perforation, as insufflated air worsens it.

visual.title: Kwame's erect chest X-ray
visual.caption: Crescents of gas under both hemidiaphragms: pneumoperitoneum.

steps.text: Sitting him upright for at least 10 minutes lets the free gas rise under the diaphragm.

steps.title: Kwame's bloods
steps.text: Raised inflammatory markers and lactate. The modest amylase rise is from leaked duodenal contents.

visual.title: Kwame's lactate
visual.label: Kwame 3.4
visual.caption: Raised lactate signals tissue hypoperfusion from sepsis; above 4 suggests septic shock.

steps.lead: The surgeons request a **CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast**: the most specific test, showing **extraluminal gas and fluid** around Kwame's duodenum.

steps.text: A normal erect CXR does **not** exclude perforation. If suspicion stays high, go to **CT**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (NBM, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, urgent surgical review) or definitive surgery: omental patch for a perforated ulcer, Hartmann's for sigmoid perforation with sepsis.

steps.lead: Kwame is made **NBM**, given oxygen, IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and analgesia; an **NG tube** goes down as he is nauseated.

visual.title: Kwame over the first 4 hours
visual.caption: Heart rate climbs and BP falls as sepsis sets in: hypotension is a late sign and means theatre now.

steps.lead: Kwame now has **hypotension, sepsis and peritonitis** together: a surgical emergency needing immediate intervention.

steps.q: Which is the definitive operation for Kwame's perforated duodenal ulcer?
steps.r: **Omental patch repair** plugs the hole with omentum. Hartmann's is for sigmoid perforation.

steps.lead: Kwame has a laparotomy, **washout** and **omental patch repair**. A sigmoid perforation with sepsis would instead need a **Hartmann's procedure**.

steps.title: Kwame's pathway
nodes: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, analgesia, NG tube
Erect CXR then CT: free gas confirmed
Urgent surgery: washout and omental patch
After: stop NSAIDs, PPI, test and treat H. pylori
steps.caption: Resuscitate and operate in parallel; do not delay theatre for perfect imaging when he is shocked.

steps.text: Do not send a suspected perforation for **upper GI endoscopy**. The air pumped in can enlarge the hole; endoscopy comes weeks later to check healing.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: how NSAIDs or H. pylori cause ulcer perforation, why free air appears under the diaphragm, or why Hartmann's avoids an anastomosis.

steps.lead: Acid, bile and bacteria from Kwame's duodenum poured into his peritoneal cavity, causing a **chemical then bacterial peritonitis**.

steps.q: How did ibuprofen cause Kwame's ulcer?
steps.r: Less **prostaglandin** means less mucus, less bicarbonate and poorer mucosal blood flow, so acid digests the wall.

steps.lead: Kwame's **NSAID** stripped his protective mucosal barrier; acid and pepsin then digested through the full thickness of the wall.

steps.title: From NSAID to peritonitis
nodes: NSAID or H. pylori damages the mucosal barrier
Gas and contents leak into the peritoneum

steps.lead: The gas under Kwame's diaphragm on his erect CXR escaped from the duodenal lumen and rose to the highest point of his peritoneal cavity.
Joining bowel in a **contaminated, septic** abdomen risks a leak, which is why Hartmann's brings out an end colostomy instead. Untreated, perforation leads to sepsis, abscess and death.

steps.text: In typhoid, *Salmonella* Typhi invades the **Peyer's patches** of the distal ileum; their necrosis is what perforates, usually in the second or third week.

mcq.q: What is the classic abdominal sign of a perforated viscus?
mcq.r: Generalised peritonitis gives a **board-like** rigid abdomen.

mcq.q: Which drug history classically precedes a perforated peptic ulcer?
mcq.r: **NSAIDs** (and H. pylori) are the main risk factors.

mcq.q: Typhoid causes perforation of which part of the bowel?
mcq.r: Necrosis of **Peyer's patches** in the distal ileum.

mcq.q: Which drug should be avoided in mechanical bowel obstruction because it can precipitate perforation?
mcq.r: **Metoclopramide** is a prokinetic and raises pressure behind the obstruction.

mcq.q: What is the initial investigation for suspected perforation?
mcq.r: **Erect CXR** looks for free air under the diaphragm.

mcq.q: What is the most specific investigation for GI perforation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
mcq.r: **CT** shows extraluminal gas or fluid and the likely site.

mcq.q: Which is the surgical repair for a perforated peptic ulcer?
Which operation is used for sigmoid perforation with sepsis?
mcq.r: **Hartmann's**: sigmoid resection, end colostomy, rectal stump closed.

mcq.q: Which triad makes GI perforation a surgical emergency?
Why does free air appear under the diaphragm?
o: Gas escapes from the bowel lumen into the peritoneal cavity
mcq.r: Escaped gas rises to the highest point: under the diaphragm on an erect film.

technique.stem: A 70 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has sudden, severe epigastric pain that began 3 hours ago and has spread across her abdomen. She takes naproxen daily. She is lying still and her abdomen is rigid with absent bowel sounds. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of sudden severe upper abdominal pain.
Sudden onset, NSAID use and generalised peritonitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Perforated peptic ulcer**.

elim: Cholecystitis is RUQ, gradual, with Murphy's sign.
Pancreatitis radiates to the back and is rarely board-like.
Biliary colic is colicky RUQ pain with a soft abdomen.
Reflux does not cause peritonitis.

steps.x: **E. Perforated peptic ulcer.** Rule: sudden epigastric pain + NSAID + rigid abdomen.

technique.stem: A 55 year old man has sudden, severe epigastric pain that has become generalised over 2 hours. He takes ibuprofen for back pain. His abdomen is rigid. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. He has been assessed with ABCDE and the surgical team has been called.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?

steps.x: Initial imaging for a suspected perforation.
Suspected perforated peptic ulcer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Erect chest X-ray** for free air under the diaphragm.

elim: USS is poor for free gas and used for biliary disease.
CT angiography is for mesenteric ischaemia or AAA.
Lipase is a blood test, not imaging, for pancreatitis.
Endoscopy can worsen a perforation.

steps.x: **C. Erect chest X-ray.** CT follows as the most specific test.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man returned from Pakistan 2 weeks ago. He has had fever, headache, constipation and myalgia for 12 days. Today he developed sudden severe abdominal pain and his abdomen is rigid. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. CT shows free gas near the terminal ileum.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management of a perforation in a returning traveller.

clues: free gas near the terminal ileum
steps.x: Typhoid with ileal perforation from Peyer's patch necrosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent surgery plus antibiotics**.

elim: Antibiotics alone will not close a perforation.
He is septic and perforated.
Delay is dangerous; treat now.
Perforation needs surgery.

steps.x: **E. Urgent laparotomy with IV antibiotics.** Typhoid perforation needs both.

technique.stem: A 78 year old man has perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with faecal peritonitis. His pulse rate is 128 bpm and BP 84/50 mmHg despite fluids. The surgeon performs a Hartmann's procedure rather than resection with primary anastomosis.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason for avoiding a primary anastomosis?
o: High risk of anastomotic leak in a contaminated, septic field
Need to preserve the rectum for radiotherapy

steps.x: Why choose Hartmann's: the reason behind the operation.
A heavily contaminated field and an unstable, septic patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An anastomosis would likely **leak**; an end colostomy avoids that.

elim: Histology is the same either way.
No cancer or radiotherapy here.
Hernia risk does not decide this.
Hartmann's needs a second operation to reverse.

steps.x: **B. Anastomotic leak risk.** Sepsis + contamination = no join.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman has sudden, severe epigastric pain that started 2 hours ago and now affects her whole abdomen. She takes naproxen for osteoarthritis. She is lying still with a rigid, silent abdomen. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden epigastric pain becoming generalised with a rigid abdomen in an NSAID user is a perforated peptic ulcer. A mildly raised amylase occurs in perforation; pancreatitis usually gives much higher levels.

steps.x: Diagnosis of sudden epigastric pain.
NSAID plus generalised peritonitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Perforated peptic ulcer**.

elim: RUQ, gradual, Murphy's sign.
Amylase is only mildly raised; pain radiates to the back.
MI does not cause a rigid abdomen.
AAA gives back pain, a pulsatile mass and shock.

steps.x: **D. Perforated peptic ulcer.** Small amylase rises happen in perforation.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man had a colonoscopy with removal of a large sigmoid polyp this morning. Four hours later he has increasing abdominal pain, distension and fever. He is tender with guarding. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 122/72 mmHg. Erect chest X-ray (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Peritonism and free air under the diaphragm after colonoscopy is iatrogenic colonic perforation. Post-polypectomy bleeding causes rectal bleeding, not free gas.

steps.x: Diagnosis after a procedure, with an X-ray to interpret.

clues: colonoscopy with removal of a large sigmoid polyp
steps.x: Iatrogenic injury is a recognised cause; the CXR shows pneumoperitoneum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Colonic perforation**.

elim: Pancreatitis follows ERCP, not colonoscopy, and gives no free gas.
Ischaemic colitis gives bloody diarrhoea, not free air.
Bleeding gives blood per rectum and anaemia.
Volvulus gives a coffee-bean sign on AXR.

steps.x: **B. Colonic perforation.** Free air after a scope = perforation.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman with known diverticular disease has had 3 days of left iliac fossa pain. This afternoon the pain became severe and spread across her whole abdomen. She has generalised guarding. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg. An erect chest X-ray shows gas under the diaphragm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: LIF pain progressing to generalised peritonitis, septic shock and free gas is perforated diverticulitis. An abscess stays localised.

steps.x: Diagnosis: what has diverticulitis turned into?
Diverticulitis that has ruptured: free gas and generalised peritonitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Perforated diverticulitis**.

elim: Abscess gives a localised mass and swinging fever, not generalised peritonitis.
Ischaemic colitis gives bloody diarrhoea, not free gas.
Volvulus gives massive distension and constipation.
Uncomplicated disease has no free gas or peritonitis.

steps.x: **C. Perforated diverticulitis.**

practice.stem: A 30 year old man returned from Bangladesh 3 weeks ago. He has had a 2 week history of rising fever, headache, dry cough, fatigue and constipation. Today he has sudden severe lower abdominal pain and a rigid abdomen. His temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. CT shows free gas near the terminal ileum.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Typhoid fever (Salmonella Typhi) causes necrosis of Peyer's patches in the distal ileum, leading to perforation. The relative bradycardia for his fever is another typhoid clue.

steps.x: Organism behind an ileal perforation.

clues: rising fever, headache, dry cough, fatigue and constipation
free gas near the terminal ileum
steps.x: Enteric fever picture, then ileal perforation. Pulse is low for a temperature of 39.6°C.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Salmonella Typhi**, via Peyer's patch necrosis.

elim: Campylobacter gives bloody diarrhoea, rarely perforates.
C. difficile follows antibiotics and perforates the colon via toxic megacolon.
Amoebiasis affects the colon and liver.
Shigella causes dysentery of the colon.

steps.x: **D. Salmonella Typhi.** Fever + constipation + ileal perforation.

practice.stem: An 80 year old woman is admitted with large bowel obstruction from a sigmoid tumour. She is vomiting and a new antiemetic is started. Six hours later she has sudden severe abdominal pain and becomes peritonitic. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. CT shows free intraperitoneal gas.
practice.q: Which medication is most likely to have contributed?
practice.e: Metoclopramide, a prokinetic dopamine antagonist, increases pressure behind a mechanical obstruction and can precipitate perforation. Cyclizine is the usual antiemetic choice in obstruction.

steps.x: Which drug caused the perforation?
A prokinetic given in mechanical obstruction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metoclopramide**.

elim: Cyclizine is not prokinetic; it is the preferred antiemetic in obstruction.
Morphine slows the gut.
Ondansetron is not prokinetic.
Paracetamol has no gut motor effect.

steps.x: **B. Metoclopramide.** Never give a prokinetic in mechanical obstruction.

practice.stem: A 49 year old man with known H. pylori infection, never treated, has had sudden epigastric pain for 3 hours. He vomited dark material once. His temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. He is reluctant to move.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
o: Board-like rigidity with absent bowel sounds
Soft abdomen with tinkling bowel sounds
practice.e: A perforated peptic ulcer causes generalised chemical peritonitis, so the abdomen is board-like and silent. Cullen's sign is periumbilical bruising in haemorrhagic pancreatitis.

steps.x: A finding question: what will you feel?
Peptic ulcer risk, sudden pain, coffee-ground vomit, peritonism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Board-like rigidity**, reduced or absent bowel sounds.

elim: Cullen's is haemorrhagic pancreatitis.
Palpable gallbladder with jaundice suggests pancreatic cancer.
Pulsatile mass is an AAA.
Tinkling sounds suggest obstruction, not peritonitis.

steps.x: **A. Board-like rigidity.**

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has sudden severe epigastric pain and a rigid abdomen. He takes aspirin and ibuprofen. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. He sits upright for 10 minutes and an erect chest X-ray is taken.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on his erect chest X-ray?
practice.e: Pneumoperitoneum shows as gas under the diaphragm on an erect film, the classic sign of a perforated viscus. Sitting upright first lets the gas collect there.

steps.x: Investigation finding in suspected perforation.
Perforated ulcer suspected; the film is taken upright so gas rises.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Free air under the diaphragm**.

elim: Hilar nodes suggest sarcoidosis or lymphoma.
Collapse is a lung problem.
Effusion can follow pancreatitis but is not the perforation sign.
Widened mediastinum suggests aortic dissection.

steps.x: **B. Free air under the diaphragm.** Pneumoperitoneum.

practice.stem: A 60 year old woman has 6 hours of severe abdominal pain with guarding and tachycardia. Her erect chest X-ray shows no free air, but the surgical team remains concerned about perforation. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
practice.e: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the gold standard, most specific test, showing extraluminal gas or fluid. A normal erect CXR does not exclude perforation.

steps.x: Diagnostic (gold standard) test after a negative CXR.

clues: erect chest X-ray shows no free air
steps.x: CXR misses some perforations; suspicion is still high.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast**.

elim: Barium leaking into the peritoneum is harmful.
Enemas risk worsening a colonic perforation.
MRI is slow and less available acutely.
Endoscopy can enlarge a perforation.

steps.x: **C. CT with IV contrast.** Gold standard, most specific.

practice.stem: A 57 year old man has sudden severe epigastric pain and a rigid abdomen. He takes diclofenac. Erect chest X-ray shows free air under the diaphragm. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 114 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. He feels nauseated.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Admission with NBM, IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review
practice.e: Initial management is NBM, oxygen, IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, analgesia, an NG tube for nausea and urgent surgical review. Endoscopy and barium are dangerous in perforation.

steps.x: Initial management of a confirmed perforation.
Pneumoperitoneum and peritonitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **NBM, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, analgesia, NG tube, surgeons.**

elim: Endoscopy worsens a perforation.
Eradication comes after the emergency.
Oral treatment and discharge is unsafe.
Barium in the peritoneum is harmful.

steps.x: **A. Resuscitate and call the surgeons.**

practice.stem: A 62 year old man with a perforated duodenal ulcer confirmed on CT has been resuscitated with IV fluids and antibiotics. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. He is taken to theatre.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive operation?
practice.e: A perforated peptic ulcer is repaired with an omental patch and peritoneal washout. Hartmann's is for sigmoid perforation; gastrectomy is rarely needed.

steps.x: Definitive surgery for a perforated duodenal ulcer.
Repair the hole.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Omental patch repair** with washout.

elim: Gastrectomy is a historical or last-resort operation.
Endoscopic clipping is for bleeding ulcers.
Hartmann's is for sigmoid colon perforation.
A PPI alone will not close the hole.

steps.x: **E. Omental patch repair.**

practice.stem: An 81 year old woman has perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with faecal peritonitis at laparotomy. She needed vasopressors in theatre. Her pulse rate is 130 bpm and BP 82/48 mmHg on arrival in theatre.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate operation?
practice.e: Sigmoid perforation with sepsis is managed with a Hartmann's procedure: sigmoid resection, end colostomy and rectal stump closure, avoiding a risky anastomosis.

steps.x: Operation for sigmoid perforation in a shocked patient.
Contaminated field, unstable patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hartmann's procedure**.

elim: An anastomosis in faecal peritonitis is likely to leak.
Drainage is for a localised abscess.
An ileostomy alone leaves the perforation in place.
She has faecal peritonitis and shock.

steps.x: **D. Hartmann's procedure.**

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman who takes ibuprofen daily for arthritis presents with a perforated gastric ulcer. Her H. pylori test is negative. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which her medication caused the ulcer?
o: Inhibition of COX-1 reducing protective prostaglandins
Stimulation of parietal cell proton pumps
practice.e: NSAIDs inhibit COX-1, reducing prostaglandins that maintain mucus, bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow, so acid-peptic digestion erodes the full thickness of the wall.

steps.x: Mechanism of NSAID-induced ulcer.
The NSAID is the cause, not H. pylori.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **COX-1 inhibition** reduces protective prostaglandins.

elim: Gastrin excess is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
She is H. pylori negative.
NSAIDs do not directly stimulate proton pumps.
Not the NSAID mechanism.

steps.x: **C. COX-1 inhibition.** Less prostaglandin = weaker barrier.

points.p: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast: extraluminal gas or fluid

Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and analgesia
NG tube if nausea

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match the operation to the site.

points.p: Urgent surgery: repair, resection or washout
Perforated peptic ulcer: omental patch repair

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: chemical first, then bacterial.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: barrier failure, then digestion; contamination, then leak.

points.why: NSAIDs inhibit COX-1 and protective prostaglandins.

glossary.perforation: A hole through the full thickness of the bowel or stomach wall.
glossary.full-thickness: Through every layer of the bowel wall, so contents can leak out.
glossary.pneumoperitoneum: Free gas inside the peritoneal cavity, usually from a perforated bowel.
glossary.peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum, giving a rigid, very tender abdomen.
glossary.peritoneal cavity: The space inside the abdomen lined by peritoneum.
glossary.board-like: Describes a rigid abdomen with involuntary muscle spasm from peritonitis.
glossary.guarding: Involuntary tensing of the abdominal muscles when pressed.
glossary.rebound tenderness: Pain when pressure on the abdomen is suddenly released.
glossary.peptic ulcer: An ulcer in the stomach or duodenum caused by acid and pepsin.
glossary.NSAID: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, such as ibuprofen or naproxen.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as ibuprofen or naproxen.
glossary.COX-1: Enzyme making prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining; inhibited by NSAIDs.
glossary.prostaglandins: Local hormones that maintain gastric mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow.
glossary.H. pylori: Helicobacter pylori, a stomach bacterium that causes peptic ulcers.
glossary.coffee-ground: Vomit containing altered, dark blood from the upper GI tract.
glossary.typhoid: Enteric fever caused by Salmonella Typhi, spread by contaminated food and water.
glossary.Peyer's patches: Clusters of lymphoid tissue in the distal ileum, targeted by typhoid.
glossary.ileum: The last part of the small bowel, ending at the caecum.
glossary.metoclopramide: A dopamine antagonist antiemetic that speeds gut emptying; avoid in mechanical obstruction.
glossary.prokinetic: A drug that increases gut movement.
glossary.erect chest X-ray: Chest X-ray taken with the patient upright, so free gas rises under the diaphragm.
glossary.omental patch repair: Closing a perforated ulcer by stitching a piece of omentum over the hole.
glossary.omentum: A fatty apron hanging from the stomach that can seal holes and wall off infection.
glossary.Hartmann's procedure: Resection of the sigmoid colon with an end colostomy and closed rectal stump.
glossary.anastomosis: A surgical join between two ends of bowel.
glossary.anastomotic leak: Leakage of bowel contents from a surgical join.
glossary.end colostomy: The end of the colon brought out onto the abdominal wall as a stoma.
glossary.rectal stump: The closed-off top of the rectum left behind in a Hartmann's procedure.
glossary.diverticulitis: Inflammation of bowel wall pouches (diverticula), usually in the sigmoid colon.
glossary.iatrogenic: Caused by medical treatment or a procedure.
glossary.NG tube: Nasogastric tube passed through the nose into the stomach to drain it.
glossary.lactate: A product of anaerobic metabolism; raised levels signal poor tissue perfusion.
glossary.sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by the body's response to infection.
glossary.washout: Rinsing the abdominal cavity during surgery to remove contamination.
glossary.ABCDE: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure: the structured approach to an unwell patient.
